qs.q: A 68-year-old man presents with acute influenza pneumonia. During viral entry into respiratory epithelial cells, which structural components mediate initial attachment to host sialic acid receptors?
o: Surface glycoproteins embedded in the lipid bilayer
Matrix protein 1 lining the inner viral envelope
Polymerase acidic proteins bound to viral segments
Nucleoprotein complexes protecting the viral RNA
qs.e: Hemagglutinin and neuraminidase are surface glycoproteins that facilitate viral attachment and release. Matrix and nucleoproteins are internal structural elements not involved in receptor binding.

qs.q: Antigenic shift in influenza virus is most likely to occur when:
o: A high degree of herd immunity is present in the population
A host has elevated levels of protective neutralizing antibodies
An individual receives the annual seasonal influenza vaccine
A single host is infected with two distinct influenza strains
qs.e: Co‑infection allows reassortment of segmented genomes, creating a novel HA or NA. The other scenarios do not produce shift.

qs.q: Which anti-influenza medication works via neuraminidase inhibition and must be initiated within 48 hours of symptom onset?
o: Oseltamivir acting as a selective neuraminidase inhibitor
Aciclovir functioning as a nucleoside analogue agent
Ganciclovir operating as a synthetic guanine derivative
Tenofovir working as a nucleotide reverse transcriptase
qs.e: Oseltamivir is a neuraminidase inhibitor used for influenza A and B that must be started early in the disease course. Aciclovir targets herpes viruses rather than influenza.

qs.q: What is the primary function of the neuraminidase (NA) glycoprotein spike found on the envelope of influenza viruses?
o: Cleaving sialic acid residues to enable release
Protecting the viral RNA genome from destruction
Initiating host cell signaling to allow entry
Mediating viral attachment to host cell receptors
qs.e: Neuraminidase cleaves sialic acid residues on host cells to facilitate the release and transmission of new virions. Hemagglutinin (HA) is the glycoprotein responsible for attachment.
qs.s: Medical Virology: Adenoviruses, Hemorrhagic Fever & Viral Receptors: MCQs

qs.q: Public health agencies update the formulation of the seasonal influenza vaccine every year. What is the genetic mechanism primarily responsible for seasonal flu epidemics that necessitates this annual update?
o: Viral integration into host chromosomes
Complete viral envelope lysis
Antigenic shift via genetic reassortment
Antigenic drift via minor point mutations
qs.e: Antigenic drift involves gradual point mutations in surface glycoproteins, causing seasonal epidemics and requiring yearly vaccine updates. Antigenic shift causes abrupt pandemic changes.
qs.s: Virology & Mycology: Interferons, Vaccines, Fungi, Mycetoma: MCQs

qs.q: A patient is prescribed oseltamivir for influenza. Which stage of the viral replication cycle is directly blocked by this class of drugs?
o: Attachment to host cell receptors
Uncoating of the viral capsid
Release of virions via neuraminidase
Genome replication via polymerase
qs.e: Oseltamivir and other neuraminidase inhibitors block the release stage by preventing the budding and release of new virions. Nucleoside analogues are used instead to block genome replication.
qs.s: Essential Medical Virology: Structure, Classification & Replication: MCQs

qs.q: An outbreak of influenza is treated with a class of drugs that specifically inhibits the viral neuraminidase enzyme. What is the targeted stage of the viral replication cycle for these drugs?
o: Virion budding and release from cell surface
Insertion of viral DNA into host genome
Removal of the viral capsid inside endosome
Binding of viral surface glycoproteins to host
qs.e: Neuraminidase inhibitors like oseltamivir block the release of influenza virions from the host cell surface, preventing viral spread. Attachment inhibitors block binding, and M2 ion channel blockers prevent uncoating.
qs.s: Medical Virology Semester 3 Crash Revision: MCQs

qs.q: A patient with suspected H1N1 influenza virus infection requires confirmation. Which laboratory test directly detects viral genetic material for H1N1?
o: Urine antigen test
H1N1 PCR RNA
Sputum Gram stain
Rapid Ag test
qs.e: H1N1 PCR RNA is utilized specifically to detect viral RNA for H1N1 confirmation. Rapid antigen tests detect influenza antigens from nasopharyngeal swabs but do not specifically test for H1N1 RNA.

ai.title: Influenza
ai.subject: Microbiology & immunology
ai.summary: Influenza is an acute viral respiratory illness caused by orthomyxoviruses. In low‑resource settings it mimics malaria, pneumonia and bacterial sepsis; rapid clinical assessment and supportive care are key.

sections.p: Influenza is a self‑limited infection of the upper and lower respiratory tract caused by influenza A or B viruses. In East Africa it often presents with fever, myalgia, cough and can be complicated by bacterial pneumonia, especially in malnourished or HIV‑positive patients.
b: High attack rate in children and young adults

sections.p: Orthomyxoviruses are enveloped, segmented, negative‑sense RNA viruses with haemagglutinin (HA) and neuraminidase (NA) surface proteins. Antigenic drift leads to yearly vaccine updates.
Spread by respiratory droplets and fomites. Virus enters ciliated epithelium, replicates, and is shed for 5–7 days. In low‑resource settings, crowded housing and lack of hand hygiene increase spread.
Typical influenza causes fever, myalgia, sore throat, dry cough and malaise. Severe disease includes viral pneumonia, ARDS and secondary bacterial pneumonia. In HIV or malnutrition, mortality rises.
b: Bacterial superinfection mainly S. pneumoniae, S. aureus, Klebsiella

sections.p: Clinical diagnosis is based on sudden onset of fever, myalgia and cough. In low‑resource settings rapid antigen tests are often unavailable; a simple clinical score can guide treatment.
b: Influenza‑like illness (ILI) definition: fever >38 °C + cough or sore throat, onset <7 days

t.b: A positive result supports antiviral therapy; a negative result still warrants treatment if clinical suspicion is high
Positive confirms strain and guides public health response

sections.p: Supportive care is mainstay. Antivirals (oseltamivir) are recommended within 48 h of symptom onset, especially in high‑risk groups. Vaccination is the cornerstone of prevention.
b: Avoid NSAIDs in severe cases due to bleeding risk

sections.p: On exam, look for rapid onset, high fever, myalgia, dry cough and conjunctivitis. In low‑resource settings, a simple ILI score plus history of recent contact can guide empiric therapy. Remember that bacterial pneumonia may present with productive cough, pleuritic chest pain and hypoxia.
b: Do not delay antiviral therapy beyond 48 h in high‑risk patients

whenToSeekHelp: Severe hypoxia (SpO₂ <90%), respiratory distress, confusion, persistent vomiting, haemoptysis, shock

faq.a: Rarely, influenza can cause transient hepatitis, but it is not a common complication.
Yes, it is considered safe; benefits outweigh risks in severe influenza.

faq.q: Do I need a chest X‑ray for all influenza patients?
faq.a: Only if there are signs of pneumonia, hypoxia or severe disease; otherwise, clinical assessment suffices.

exam: A 28‑year‑old HIV‑positive woman presents with fever, cough and chest pain. What is the next best step? — Start empiric antibiotics (ceftriaxone + azithromycin) and consider oseltamivir if within 48 h; obtain chest X‑ray if hypoxia or pleuritic pain.

A patient with influenza develops sudden haemoptysis. What is the most likely diagnosis and management? — Post‑influenza bacterial pneumonia (often S. aureus); start IV vancomycin + ceftriaxone, monitor airway.

A child with influenza has persistent fever after 5 days. What is the most appropriate investigation? — Rapid antigen test if available; otherwise, consider bacterial superinfection and start empiric antibiotics.
An elderly patient with influenza has SpO₂ 88% on room air. What is the immediate management? — Oxygen therapy to >94%, consider ICU transfer if no improvement.
A 35‑year‑old man with influenza is allergic to penicillin. What antibiotic should you use for suspected bacterial pneumonia? — Azithromycin alone or doxycycline if atypical organisms are suspected.
A patient with influenza is on chronic NSAIDs. What is the concern? — NSAIDs increase bleeding risk and may mask fever; consider acetaminophen instead.
A pregnant woman with influenza is concerned about antiviral safety. What do you advise? — Oseltamivir is safe in pregnancy; benefits outweigh risks.
